summary: The article, dated September 5, 2023, describes record labor shortages hitting small businesses in the US as unemployment falls and wages rise. It profiles owners and experts who respond by tapping underused talent pools, adopting e-learning, emphasizing culture and work-life balance, partnering locally, using reskilling grants and apprenticeships, and allowing remote work. It concludes that adaptation, technology, and community collaboration can help small businesses build sustainable paths forward.
one_line: Small businesses facing 2023 labor shortages are responding with new talent pools, training technology, better culture, partnerships, apprenticeships, and remote work.
key_facts: The article is dated September 5, 2023, and describes unprecedented labor shortages across small businesses nationwide.
Unemployment rates have fallen to record lows since mid-2023, causing wage inflation that strains small enterprises' narrow margins.
James O'Neill, a local economic analyst from Springfield, Michigan, describes a 'triple-threat scenario': high demand for labor, decreased availability of labor, and an escalating wage market.
Megha Singh, CEO of 'TechSolutions' in Austin, Texas, found a wealth of talent among retirees by broadening her search.
Sarah Chen, training coordinator at 'Circuit Hive' (an electronics retailer in Sacramento, California), says investment in e-learning bridged the skill gap and improved engagement and retention.
A Catalytics Consulting Group survey released September 20, 2023, found that 60% of workers would forego a pay hike for better work-life balance and a positive workplace culture.
Harold Katz of 'Katz Delicatessen' in New York says staff turnover has decreased by 25% since last year after focusing on making employees feel valued and heard.
Amanda Lui, President of the 'Juliana Ville Small Business Association,' says shared job fairs and community training programs help downtown businesses attract talent.
'New Horizons Bakers' in Atlanta benefited from a pilot reskilling program funded by a government grant received on September 30, 2023, training staff in advanced baking and pastry arts.
Roberta Jefferson, a Seattle immigration lawyer, said on October 1, 2023, that clear employment paths for immigrants can ease pressure on small business labor markets.
Maryland's 'Charm City Craftsmen,' led by CEO Mike Anderson, partners with a local vocational school for hands-on apprenticeship training.
Allison DeMarco of 'Allison's Artisan Breads' in Denver says offering remote work options vastly expanded her talent pool.
